plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: Just as the meadows turn gold, goblet-shaped lavender-pink blooms push straight out of bare ground with no leaves in sight. The leaves appeared months earlier and have long since died back. The flowers look like delicate, tulip-like crocuses scattered across damp grassland.
plants.funFact: Despite the name, it isn't a true crocus. It is toxic, and it is the source of colchicine, a compound used in medicine and in plant breeding.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: The largest bloom in the protea family is a bowl-shaped flower head up to 30 cm across. It has a crown of silky pink-tipped bracts around a center that looks like a thistle. It stands out against the fynbos shrubland of the Cape.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mainly winter and spring (June to October)
plants.location: Fynbos of the Western Cape, South Africa, including Kirstenbosch gardens
plants.funFact: It is South Africa's national flower. It belongs to an ancient plant family that dates back to when the southern continents were joined as Gondwana.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: Australia's national floral emblem is a fragrant shrub or small tree that bursts into clouds of fluffy, bright golden pom-poms in late winter and early spring. Each blossom ball is made up of dozens of tiny flowers.
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, including South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales
plants.funFact: Each golden ball holds roughly 40 to 80 tiny flowers. Gold and green are Australia's national colors, and the wattle displays both when it blooms.

plants.name: Cosmos bipinnatus
plants.description: A cheerful annual with feathery foliage and daisy-like flowers on tall, airy stems. In late summer, cosmos turns sunny borders into drifts of pink, white and crimson that bees and butterflies love.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer into fall (August to September and beyond)
plants.location: Gardens across temperate North America and Europe, native to Mexico
plants.funFact: Cosmos comes from a Greek word meaning 'order' or 'harmony'. It is also easy to grow, and it thrives in poor, dry soil.
